title: Sana Ullah Khan- VS -FOP etc.
text:
Form No: HCJD/C-121. 
ORDER SHEET. 
IN  THE  ISLAMABAD HIGH  COURT, ISLAMABAD. 
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT. 
 
Criminal Misc. No. 1919-B of 2025 
Muhammad Umer Farooq 
 
Versus 
 
The State & another  
 
S. No. of order/ 
proceedings
Date of  order/
Proceedings
Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or 
counsel where necessary.
 
05.01.2026. 
Mr. Estasham Aslam Khan, Advocate for the petitioner.  
Complainant in person. 
Ms. Shaista Tabassum, Assistant Attorney General. 
Mr. Mohsin Hassan, S.I/FIA.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The petitioner [Muhammad Umer Farooq] 
has sought bail after-arrest in case, F.I.R. 
No.95/2025, dated 20.05.2025, registered under 
sections 489-F & 406 of Pakistan Penal Code, 
1860 ("PPC") at Police Station FIA/AHTC, 
Islamabad. 
2. 
As per the FIR, the complainant alleged 
that the accused/petitioner, along with co-accused 
persons, received an amount of Rs.75,63,000/- 
from the complainant’s father and others for 
arranging Hajj. It is alleged that the petitioner 
failed to fulfill the said obligation and, after 
returning a partial amount of Rs.14,00,000/-, 
issued cheques amounting to Rs.74,88,000/- as 
guarantee, 
which 
were 
dishonoured 
upon 
presentation, thereby committing criminal breach 
of trust and an offence under Section 489-F PPC. 
3. 
Learned 
counsel 
for 
the 
petitioner 
contended that the petitioner has been falsely 
implicated with mala fide intent; that the cheques 
in question were issued merely as security

Crl. Misc No. 1919-B of 2025         
                        2 | P a g e  
 
pursuant to an agreement and were not meant for 
encashment; that the dispute is civil in nature and 
has been given a criminal colour; and that the 
petitioner has already returned a substantial 
amount through banking channels. It was further 
argued that the offence does not fall within the 
prohibitory clause of Section 497 Cr.P.C., and 
thus the petitioner is entitled to the concession of 
bail. 
4. 
Conversely, learned Assistant Attorney 
General assisted by the Sub-Inspector, FIA, 
opposed the bail petition, contending that the 
petitioner is specifically nominated in the FIR; 
that issuance of cheques and execution of 
agreement are not disputed; that the cheques were 
dishonoured; and that sufficient material is 
available on record to connect the petitioner with 
the alleged offences. It was argued that mere non-
applicability of the prohibitory clause does not 
automatically entitle the petitioner to bail. 
5. 
Arguments heard and record perused. 
6. 
At the bail stage, only a tentative 
assessment of the material is permissible and 
deeper appreciation of evidence is to be avoided. 
For attracting Section 489-F PPC, the prosecution 
is required to prima facie establish that the 
cheque was issued with dishonest intention at the 
time of issuance, in discharge of a loan or legal 
obligation, and that it was dishonoured. Mere 
issuance of cheques and their dishonour, by 
themselves, do not automatically constitute an 
offence unless mens rea is shown to exist from 
the inception.

Crl. Misc No. 1919-B of 2025         
                        3 | P a g e  
 
7. 
In the present case, it is not disputed that 
the transaction arose out of an arrangement for 
provision of services, that partial amount has 
already been returned, and that the cheques were 
issued 
in 
continuation 
of 
the 
underlying 
arrangement. Whether the cheques were issued as 
security or towards discharge of a legally 
enforceable liability, and whether dishonest 
intention existed at the relevant time, are matters 
requiring recording of evidence and cannot be 
conclusively determined at the bail stage. 
Similarly, with regard to Section 406 PPC, the 
question whether the petitioner acted dishonestly 
in misappropriating the entrusted amount or 
whether the dispute essentially pertains to non-
performance of a contractual obligation, is also a 
matter to be adjudicated after trial. At this stage, 
the available material calls for further inquiry 
within the meaning of Section 497(2) Cr.P.C. 
8. 
It is also pertinent to note that the 
maximum punishment provided for the alleged 
offences does not bring the case within the 
prohibitory clause of Section 497(1) Cr.P.C. It is 
settled law that in offences not falling within the 
prohibitory clause, grant of bail is a rule and 
refusal an exception, particularly where the 
controversy appears to be rooted in a civil or 
commercial transaction. 
9. 
Keeping 
in 
view 
the 
totality 
of 
circumstances, the nature of allegations, the 
partial return of amount, the documentary nature 
of the evidence, and without expressing any 
opinion on the merits of the case, this Court is of 
the view that the petitioner has made out a case

Crl. Misc No. 1919-B of 2025         
                        4 | P a g e  
 
for concession of post-arrest bail. Consequently, 
the petition is allowed and the petitioner 
Muhammad Umer Farooq is admitted to post-
arrest bail in the above-mentioned case, subject to 
furnishing bail bond in the sum of Rs.5,00,000/- 
(Rupees Five Lakh only) with one surety in the 
like amount, to the satisfaction of the learned trial 
Court. 
10. 
The observations made herein are tentative 
in nature and shall not prejudice the case of either 
party at trial.  
 
 
 
 
+ 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(Muhammad Asif) 
  Judge
